analysis.one_liner: Imposes a per-pound excise tax on new virgin plastic used in single-use products to fund cleanup and recycling.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Whitehouse with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The REDUCE Act would charge plastics makers and importers 10 to 20 cents per pound on new petroleum-based plastic resin used in single-use items like packaging, beverage containers, bags, and food service products. Recycled plastic, medical products, and hazardous-materials packaging would be exempt, and resin used in non-single-use products would get a refund. The money would go into a dedicated fund for recycling infrastructure, marine debris cleanup, and addressing pollution harms in affected communities. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near plastic production facilities and waterways affected by plastic waste, since the fund would pay for cleanup, monitoring, and environmental justice programs. Coastal communities and the fishing and tourism sectors that bear marine debris costs would also benefit, and municipalities would get help upgrading recycling infrastructure.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated Plastic Waste Reduction Fund financed by the tax, to pay for recycling infrastructure improvements, marine debris reduction and cleanup programs, and efforts to address environmental justice and pollution impacts from plastic production [S2][S3].

Taxes only new 'virgin' plastic resin derived from petroleum or gas, at 10 cents per pound in 2022 rising to 20 cents in 2024 and inflation-indexed thereafter, so recycled plastic is not taxed and the price advantage shifts toward recycled material [S3].
Exempts medical products, drug containers, infant formula, hygiene and sexual health products, and hazardous-materials packaging, so safety-critical single-use plastics are not discouraged [S3].
Refunds the tax on resin used to make products that are not single-use items, limiting the tax to the single-use waste stream, and exempts exported resin entirely [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, producers, and importers of more than 10 tons of virgin plastic resin per year would owe the tax, and importers of single-use plastic goods would owe it on covered items. Part of the cost would likely be passed to consumers through slightly higher prices on packaged goods and takeout food.

drawbacks.text: The tax is passed through the supply chain, so households would pay somewhat more for packaged food, beverages, and takeout, which weighs heaviest on lower-income consumers [S3].

A tax targeted only at single-use plastic can push manufacturers toward other single-use materials like paper or aluminum that may carry their own environmental costs, rather than reducing disposability overall [S3].
The bill left details of compliance, alternate import rates, and fund appropriations to the Treasury and future Congresses, so effectiveness would depend on later implementation choices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted the single-use plastic waste stream narrowly and carefully: recycled plastic is untaxed, safety-critical items are exempt, and non-single-use uses get refunds. The main cost is a modest price increase on disposable consumer goods, weighed against dedicated funding for cleanup and recycling in communities that bear pollution harms. It was a well-aimed but modest-scale policy that never got a substantive hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Whitehouse introduced the bill on August 5, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action; the action history records nothing after the referral, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Virgin plastic resin producers and the single-use packaging supply chain are better off because the tax never advanced; communities affected by plastic pollution gained nothing.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill; a known advocate of measures targeting plastic pollution.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to the Finance Committee, and it died there.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support typically needed to get floor time in a 50-50 Senate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no committee or floor vote was ever held, so its partisan shape is inferred from sponsorship alone.

industries.industry: Petrochemical and virgin plastic resin producers
industries.note: These companies would owe 10-20 cents per pound on new petroleum-based plastic, directly reducing demand for virgin resin relative to recycled material. Their interest in the bill was squarely against the public's interest in less plastic waste.

industries.industry: Single-use packaging and consumer goods companies
industries.note: Importers of single-use plastic goods would owe tax on covered items and would likely pass some cost to consumers, but the bill encourages a shift to recycled inputs and exempts many categories. Their benefit came from the bill dying.

The Plastic Waste Reduction Fund would finance recycling infrastructure improvements, expanding demand for recycled processing. This aligns with the public interest in less waste, though it would channel public money through private recyclers.

The tax applies only to resin derived from petroleum or gas, nudging demand away from oil and gas feedstocks. Lower petrochemical demand is a cost to the industry and a benefit to pollution reduction.
